instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

listeningScripts.title: Restaurant Reservation Issue
listeningScripts.text: Diner: Hi, I made a reservation for tonight at 7 PM under the name Anderson, and I just realized the name is spelled wrong in your system. Manager: Oh no, I'm sorry about that. Let me look that up. How is it spelled? Diner: A-N-D-E-R-S-O-N. I don't know how it got misspelled. Manager: I see it here as A-N-D-E-R-S-E-N. That's an easy mix-up. When you arrive, just let the host know and we'll get you seated right away. Diner: Actually, I'm calling because I need to change the time. Can I do 7:30 instead? Manager: Absolutely. Let me adjust that for you. How many people? Diner: Six of us. Manager: Perfect. I've moved you from 7 PM to 7:30 PM for six people, and I've corrected the name spelling. Is there anything else? Diner: Yes, one more thing. Can you make sure we have a quiet table? There are some business matters we want to discuss. Manager: I'll add a note to your reservation requesting a quieter area away from the bar. We have some nice tables by the window. Diner: That sounds great. What's your cancellation policy? Manager: We require 24 hours notice for cancellations. If you need to cancel, just call us before 7:30 PM tomorrow. Diner: Got it. Thank you.

listeningScripts.title: Neighbourhood Park Chat
listeningScripts.text: David: Hey, nice day, isn't it? Rebecca: Beautiful. Perfect weather for being outside. David: Have you lived in this neighbourhood long? Rebecca: About five years now. And you? David: Just moved here last month. Rebecca: Oh nice. You picked a good time to arrive. The summer's the best season here. David: So I'm hearing. Any recommendations for places to go? Rebecca: There's a great farmer's market on Saturday mornings at the corner of Main and Oak. The coffee shop near there is amazing too. David: Sounds good. I'll have to check it out. Rebecca: You definitely should. They have the best pastries. Oh, and the park just got new playground equipment if you have kids. David: No kids yet, but that's nice to know. Do many families live here? Rebecca: Lots of young families. It's a very friendly community. David: That's what I was hoping for. I'm looking forward to exploring more.

listeningScripts.title: Workplace Safety Training: Fire Procedures
listeningScripts.text: Good morning. This is your mandatory workplace fire safety training. Please listen carefully. In case of fire alarm, first, stay calm. Second, evacuate using the nearest exit. Do not use elevators under any circumstances. Stairs are located at both ends of each hallway. Third, move to the designated assembly point in the parking lot north of the building. Check in with your team leader. Fourth, do not re-enter the building until an authorized person announces it's safe. Fire drills occur quarterly on the first Friday of March, June, September, and December at 2 PM. During drills, the process is identical to a real emergency. Everyone must participate. If you cannot evacuate due to disability, proceed to a designated refuge area and use the emergency call button. These refuge areas are marked on building maps. Fire extinguishers are located every twenty-five meters along hallways and near kitchen areas. Only trained staff should operate extinguishers. If you're not trained, alert a supervisor. Report any fire hazards such as blocked exits or damaged equipment to maintenance immediately. Violations of fire safety procedures may result in disciplinary action. Contact Safety Services with any questions.

listeningScripts.title: New Tech Campus Opens in Calgary
listeningScripts.text: A major technology development is happening in Calgary today. TechHub Prairie, a 50,000-square-meter innovation center, officially opened its doors this morning in the downtown core. The facility cost 85 million dollars to construct and is expected to create 1,200 new jobs over the next two years. The campus features office space, research laboratories, and startup incubator units. Over 40 companies have already committed to moving in, including software firms, AI research groups, and digital marketing agencies. Mayor Jyoti Gondek attended the ribbon-cutting ceremony and called it a game-changer for Alberta's economy. The provincial government provided 15 million dollars in funding to support the project. TechHub Prairie will also host weekly networking events and offer mentorship programs for emerging entrepreneurs. Officials believe this development positions Calgary as a serious competitor in Canada's tech industry.

listeningScripts.title: Small Business Loan Program Discussion
listeningScripts.text:
Bank Manager Chris: Our small business loan program has been quite successful this year. We've approved 285 loans totaling 42 million dollars to local entrepreneurs. However, we've noticed our default rate is slightly higher than industry average at about 4.2 percent. We're considering tightening our lending criteria to reduce risk.

Economic Development Officer Lisa: I would caution against tightening the criteria too much, Chris. These small loans are crucial for community development and job creation. Yes, a few borrowers struggle, but 95 percent of our loans are performing well. If we make the qualification requirements too strict, we'll only serve well-established businesses with existing collateral. That defeats the purpose of supporting new entrepreneurs who are taking real risks.

Business Owner Marcus: I completely agree with Lisa. When I started my restaurant five years ago, traditional banks wouldn't touch me because I didn't have significant assets or a ten-year track record. Your bank took a chance on me, and now my business employs 12 people. If your criteria were stricter, I wouldn't be here. I think what you should focus on is better support systems after lending, like mentorship programs and financial coaching.

Bank Manager Chris: Marcus, your success story is exactly what we want to see. But we do have a fiduciary responsibility to our depositors. Maybe Marcus is right—perhaps the answer isn't stricter lending, but better support after approval. We could partner with business development organizations to provide mentoring and financial management training.

listeningScripts.title: Universal Basic Income Feasibility
listeningScripts.text: I want to discuss Universal Basic Income, or UBI, and why I believe it could work in Canada. The concept is straightforward: every citizen receives a regular, unconditional cash payment from the government. Now, I know people immediately worry about the cost, but let me address that. First, UBI could replace many existing welfare programs that are expensive to administer. The bureaucracy involved in means-testing and eligibility verification costs billions. UBI would be simpler and less wasteful. Second, the economic stimulus of putting money in people's hands is significant. When people have financial security, they spend more, which supports businesses and creates jobs. Third, UBI addresses real problems: poverty, economic instability, and lack of opportunity. We've seen pilot projects in Kenya, Finland, and Canada that show positive outcomes. In Kenya, UBI increased business formation by 32 percent. In Finland, participants reported better mental health and less anxiety. Some worry it will make people lazy, but that's not supported by evidence. People want purpose and contribution, not just money. What UBI does is give them the freedom to pursue education, care for family, or start businesses without desperation. The real question isn't whether we can afford UBI—it's whether we can afford not to implement it. Rising inequality and automation are creating unprecedented challenges.
